entries.43b6d12d276c784e068b4793531b65d49efa90ad: <div sID="gen3309" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="33" osisID="Num.33" sID="Num.33"/> <div eID="gen3309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3310" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3311" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. A particular account of the removals and encampments of the children of Israel, from their escape out of Egypt to their entrance into Canaan, forty-two in all, with some remarkable events that happened at some of those places, <reference osisRef="Num.33.1-Num.33.49">ver. 1-49</reference>. II. A strict command given them to drive out all the inhabitants of the land of Canaan, which they were not going to conquer and take possession of, <reference osisRef="Num.33.50-Num.33.56">ver. 50-56</reference>. So that the former part of the chapter looks back upon their march through the wilderness, the latter looks forward to their settlement in Canaan.
entries.5213454a8d313f76ac3e1911ba69ef2d3fd5ac41: <div eID="gen3311" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3310" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Encampments of the Israelites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1452.)</title> <div sID="gen3312" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the journeys of the children of Israel, which went forth out of the land of Egypt with their armies under the hand of Moses and Aaron. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Moses wrote their goings out according to their journeys by the commandment of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and these <hi type="italic">are</hi> their journeys according to their goings out. <hi type="super">3</hi> And they departed from Rameses in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the first month; on the morrow after the passover the children of Israel went out with an high hand in the sight of all the Egyptians. <hi type="super">4</hi> For the Egyptians buried all <hi type="italic">their</hi> firstborn, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had smitten among them: upon their gods also the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> executed judgments. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the children of Israel removed from Rameses, and pitched in Succoth. <hi type="super">6</hi> And they departed from Succoth, and pitched in Etham, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the edge of the wilderness. <hi type="super">7</hi> And they removed from Etham, and turned again unto Pi-hahiroth, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> before Baal-zephon: and they pitched before Migdol. <hi type="super">8</hi> And they departed from before Pi-hahiroth, and passed through the midst of the sea into the wilderness, and went three days' journey in the wilderness of Etham, and pitched in Marah. <hi type="super">9</hi> And they removed from Marah, and came unto Elim: and in Elim <hi type="italic">were</hi> twelve fountains of water, and threescore and ten palm trees; and they pitched there. 10 And they removed from Elim, and encamped by the Red sea. 11 And they removed from the Red sea, and encamped in the wilderness of Sin. <hi type="super">12</hi> And they took their journey out of the wilderness of Sin, and encamped in Dophkah. <hi type="super">13</hi> And they departed from Dophkah, and encamped in Alush. <hi type="super">14</hi> And they removed from Alush, and encamped at Rephidim, where was no water for the people to drink. <hi type="super">15</hi> And they departed from Rephidim, and pitched in the wilderness of Sinai. <hi type="super">16</hi> And they removed from the desert of Sinai, and pitched at Kibroth-hattaavah. <hi type="super">17</hi> And they departed from Kibroth-hattaavah, and encamped at Hazeroth. <hi type="super">18</hi> And they departed from Hazeroth, and pitched in Rithmah. <hi type="super">19</hi> And they departed from Rithmah, and pitched at Rimmon-parez. <hi type="super">20</hi> And they departed from Rimmon-parez, and pitched in Libnah. <hi type="super">21</hi> And they removed from Libnah, and pitched at Rissah. <hi type="super">22</hi> And they journeyed from Rissah, and pitched in Kehelathah. <hi type="super">23</hi> And they went from Kehelathah, and pitched in mount Shapher. <hi type="super">24</hi> And they removed from mount Shapher, and encamped in Haradah. <hi type="super">25</hi> And they removed from Haradah, and pitched in Makheloth. <hi type="super">26</hi> And they removed from Makheloth, and encamped at Tahath. <hi type="super">27</hi> And they departed from Tahath, and pitched at Tarah. <hi type="super">28</hi> And they removed from Tarah, and pitched in Mithcah. <hi type="super">29</hi> And they went from Mithcah, and pitched in Hashmonah. <hi type="super">30</hi> And they departed from Hashmonah, and encamped at Moseroth. <hi type="super">31</hi> And they departed from Moseroth, and pitched in Bene-jaakan. <hi type="super">32</hi> And they removed from Bene-jaakan, and encamped at Hor-hagidgad. <hi type="super">33</hi> And they went from Hor-hagidgad, and pitched in Jotbathah. <hi type="super">34</hi> And they removed from Jotbathah, and encamped at Ebronah. <hi type="super">35</hi> And they departed from Ebronah, and encamped at Ezion-gaber. 36 And they removed from Ezion-gaber, and pitched in the wilderness of Zin, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Kadesh. <hi type="super">37</hi> And they removed from Kadesh, and pitched in mount Hor, in the edge of the land of Edom. <hi type="super">38</hi> And Aaron the priest went up into mount Hor at the commandment of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and died there, in the fortieth year after the children of Israel were come out of the land of Egypt, in the first <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the fifth month. <hi type="super">39</hi> And Aaron <hi type="italic">was</hi> an hundred and twenty and three years old when he died in mount Hor. <hi type="super">40</hi> And king Arad the Canaanite, which dwelt in the south in the land of Canaan, heard of the coming of the children of Israel. <hi type="super">41</hi> And they departed from mount Hor, and pitched in Zalmonah. <hi type="super">42</hi> And they departed from Zalmonah, and pitched in Punon. <hi type="super">43</hi> And they departed from Punon, and pitched in Oboth. <hi type="super">44</hi> And they departed from Oboth, and pitched in Ije-abarim, in the border of Moab. <hi type="super">45</hi> And they departed from Iim, and pitched in Dibon-gad. <hi type="super">46</hi> And they removed from Dibon-gad, and encamped in Almon-diblathaim. <hi type="super">47</hi> And they removed from Almon-diblathaim, and pitched in the mountains of Abarim, before Nebo. <hi type="super">48</hi> And they departed from the mountains of Abarim, and pitched in the plains of Moab by Jordan <hi type="italic">near</hi> Jericho. <hi type="super">49</hi> And they pitched by Jordan, from Beth-jesimoth <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto Abel-shittim in the plains of Moab. <div eID="gen3312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3313" type="x-p"/> This is a review and brief rehearsal of the travels of the children of Israel through the wilderness. It was a memorable history and well worthy to be thus abridged, and the abridgment thus preserved, to the honour of God that led them and for the encouragement of the generations that followed. Observe here, <div eID="gen3313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3314" type="x-p"/> I. How the account was kept: <hi type="italic">Moses wrote their goings out,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.33.2">v. 2</reference>. When they began this tedious march, God ordered him to keep a journal or diary, and to insert in it all the remarkable occurrences of their way, that it might be a satisfaction to himself in the review and an instruction to others when it should be published. It may be of good use to private Christians, but especially to those in public stations, to preserve in writing an account of the providences of God concerning them, the constant series of mercies they have experienced, especially those turns and changes which have made some days of their lives more remarkable. Our memories are deceitful and need this help, that we may <hi type="italic">remember all the way which the Lord our God has led us in this wilderness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.8.2">Deut. viii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen3314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3315" type="x-p"/> II. What the account itself was. It began with their departure out of Egypt, continued with their march through the wilderness, and ended in the plains of Moab, where they now lay encamped. <div eID="gen3315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3316" type="x-p"/> 1. Some things are observed here concerning their departure out of Egypt, which they are reminded of upon all occasions, as a work of wonder never to be forgotten. (1.) That they <hi type="italic">went forth with their armies</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.33.1">v. 1</reference>), rank and file, as an army with banners. (2.) Under the hand of Moses and Aaron, their guides, overseers, and rulers, under God. (3.) <hi type="italic">With a high hand,</hi> because God's hand was high that wrought for them, <hi type="italic">and in the sight of all the Egyptians,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.33.3">v. 3</reference>. They did not steal away clandestinely (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.12">Isa. lii. 12</reference>), but in defiance of their enemies, to whom God had made them such a burdensome stone that they neither could, nor would, nor durst, oppose them. (4.) They went forth while the Egyptians were burying, or at least preparing to bury, their first-born, <reference osisRef="Num.33.4">v. 4</reference>. They had a mind good enough, or rather bad enough, still to have detained the Israelites their prisoners, but God found them other work to do. They would have God's first-born buried alive, but God set them a burying their own first-born. (5.) To all the plagues of Egypt it is added here that <hi type="italic">on their gods also the Lord executed judgments.</hi> Their idols which they worshipped, it is probable, were broken down, as Dagon afterwards before the ark, so that they could not consult them about this great affair. To this perhaps there is reference, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.1">Isa. xix. 1</reference>, <hi type="italic">The idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence.</hi> <div eID="gen3316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3317" type="x-p"/> 2. Concerning their travels towards Canaan. Observe, (1.) They were continually upon the remove. When they had pitched a little while in one place they departed from that to another. Such is our state in this world; we have here no continuing city. (2.) Most of their way lay through a wilderness, uninhabited, untracked, unfurnished even with the necessaries of human life, which magnifies the wisdom and power of God, by whose wonderful conduct and bounty the thousands of Israel not only subsisted for forty years in that desolate place, but came out at least as numerous and vigorous as they went in. At first they pitched <hi type="italic">in the edge of the wilderness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.33.6">v. 6</reference>), but afterwards in the heart of it; by less difficulties God prepares his people for greater. We find them in the wilderness of Etham (<reference osisRef="Num.33.8">v. 8</reference>), of Sin (<reference osisRef="Num.33.11">v. 11</reference>), of Sinai, <reference osisRef="Num.33.15">v. 15</reference>. Our removals in this world are but from one wilderness to another. (3.) They were led to and fro, forward and backward, as in a maze or labyrinth, and yet were all the while under the direction of the pillar of cloud and fire. He led them about (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.10">Deut. xxxii. 10</reference>), and yet led them the right way, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.7">Ps. cvii. 7</reference>. The way which God takes in bringing his people to himself is always the best way, though it does not always seem to us the nearest way. (4.) Some events are mentioned in this journal, as their want of water at Rephidim (<reference osisRef="Num.33.14">v. 14</reference>), the death of Aaron (<reference osisRef="Num.33.38-Num.33.39">v. 38, 39</reference>), the insult of Arad (<reference osisRef="Num.33.40">v. 40</reference>); and the very name of <hi type="italic">Kibroth-hattaavah—the graves of lusts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.33.16">v. 16</reference>), has a story depending upon it. Thus we ought to keep in mind the providences of God concerning us and our families, us and our land, and the many instances of that divine care which has led us, and fed us, and kept us, all our days hitherto. Shittim, the place where the people sinned in the matter of Peor (<reference osisRef="Num.25.1">ch. xxv. 1</reference>), is here called <hi type="italic">Abel-shittim. Abel</hi> signifies <hi type="italic">mourning</hi> (as <reference osisRef="Gen.50.11">Gen. l. 11</reference>), and probably this place was so called from the mourning of the good people of Israel on account of that sin and of God's wrath against them for it. It was so great a mourning that it gave a name to the place.
entries.8efd2df7560d4879744799e5537f0cc52ad3b264: <div eID="gen3317" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Canaanites Doomed. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1452.)</title> <div sID="gen3318" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">50</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses in the plains of Moab by Jordan <hi type="italic">near</hi> Jericho, saying, <hi type="super">51</hi> Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When ye are passed over Jordan into the land of Canaan; <hi type="super">52</hi> Then ye shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you, and destroy all their pictures, and destroy all their molten images, and quite pluck down all their high places: <hi type="super">53</hi> And ye shall dispossess <hi type="italic">the inhabitants</hi> of the land, and dwell therein: for I have given you the land to possess it. <hi type="super">54</hi> And ye shall divide the land by lot for an inheritance among your families: <hi type="italic">and</hi> to the more ye shall give the more inheritance, and to the fewer ye shall give the less inheritance: every man's <hi type="italic">inheritance</hi> shall be in the place where his lot falleth; according to the tribes of your fathers ye shall inherit. <hi type="super">55</hi> But if ye will not drive out the inhabitants of the land from before you; then it shall come to pass, that those which ye let remain of them <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> pricks in your eyes, and thorns in your sides, and shall vex you in the land wherein ye dwell. <hi type="super">56</hi> Moreover it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> I shall do unto you, as I thought to do unto them. <div eID="gen3318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3319" type="x-p"/> While the children of Israel were in the wilderness their total separation from all other people kept them out of the way of temptation to idolatry, and perhaps this was one thing intended by their long confinement in the wilderness, that thereby the idols of Egypt might be forgotten, and the people aired (as it were) and purified from that infection, and the generation that entered Canaan might be such as never knew those depths of Satan. But now that they were to pass over Jordan they were entering again into that temptation, and therefore, 1. They are here strictly charged utterly to destroy all remnants of idolatry. They must not only <hi type="italic">drive out the inhabitants of the land,</hi> that they may possess their country, but they must deface all their idolatrous pictures and images, and <hi type="italic">pull down all their high places,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.33.52">v. 52</reference>. They must not preserve any of them, no, not as monuments of antiquity to gratify the curious, nor as ornaments of their houses, nor toys for their children to play with, but they must destroy all, both in token of their abhorrence and detestation of idolatry and to prevent their being tempted to worship those images, and the false gods represented by them, or to worship the God of Israel by such images or representations. 2. They were assured that, if they did so, God would by degrees put them in full possession of the land of promise, <reference osisRef="Num.33.53-Num.33.54">v. 53, 54</reference>. If they would keep themselves pure from the idols of Canaan, God would enrich them with the wealth of Canaan. Learn not their way, and then fear not their power. 3. They were threatened that, if they spared either the idols or the idolaters, they should be beaten with their own rod and their sin would certainly be their punishment. (1.) They would foster snakes in their own bosoms, <reference osisRef="Num.33.55">v. 55</reference>. The remnant of the Canaanites, if they made any league with them, though it were but a cessation of arms, would be <hi type="italic">pricks in their eyes and thorns in their sides,</hi> that is, they would be upon all occasions vexatious to them, insulting them, robbing them, and, to the utmost of their power, making mischief among them. We must expect trouble and affliction from that, whatever it is, which we sinfully indulge; that which we are willing should tempt us we shall find will vex us. (2.) The righteous God would turn that wheel upon the Israelites which was to have crushed the Canaanites: <hi type="italic">I shall do to you as I thought to do unto them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.33.56">v. 56</reference>. It was intended that the Canaanites should be dispossessed; but if the Israelites fell in with them, and learned their way, they should be dispossessed, for God's displeasure would justly be greater against them than against the Canaanites themselves. Let us hear this, and fear. If we do not drive sin out, sin will drive us out; if we be not the death of our lusts, our lusts will be the death of our souls.  <chapter eID="Num.33"/> <div eID="gen3319" type="x-p"/>

entries.11c5d938e68d7d0ecc99276f1112b1fb0da7e66c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1605"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 33</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Num.33.1-Num.33.15">Nu 33:1-15</reference>. Two and Forty Journeys of the Israelites--from Egypt to Sinai.</title> <div sID="gen2153" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1605"/><hi type="bold">1. These are the journeys of the children of Israel--</hi>This chapter may be said to form the winding up of the history of the travels of the Israelites through the wilderness; for the three following chapters relate to matters connected with the occupation and division of the promised land. As several apparent discrepancies will be discovered on comparing the records here given of the journeyings from Sinai with the detailed accounts of the events narrated in the Book of Exodus and the occasional notices of places that are found in that of Deuteronomy, it is probable that this itinerary comprises a list of only the most important stations in their journeys--those where they formed prolonged encampments, and whence they dispersed their flocks and herds to pasture on the adjacent plains till the surrounding herbage was exhausted. The catalogue extends from their departure out of Egypt to their arrival on the plains of Moab.<div eID="gen2153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2154" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went forth ... with their armies--</hi>that is, a vast multitude marshalled in separate companies, but regular order. <div eID="gen2154" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d8c49950777356aecf862bb2bb3c488fd1f8a67: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1606"/><div sID="gen2155" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1606"/><hi type="bold">2. Moses wrote their goings out according to their journeys by the commandment of the Lord--</hi>The wisdom of this divine order is seen in the importance of the end to which it was subservient--namely, partly to establish the truth of the history, partly to preserve a memorial of God's marvellous interpositions on behalf of Israel, and partly to confirm their faith in the prospect of the difficult enterprise on which they were entering, the invasion of Canaan. <div eID="gen2155" type="x-p"/>

Rameses--</hi>generally identified with Heroopoils, now the modern Abu-Keisheid (see on <reference osisRef="Exod.12.37">Ex 12:37</reference>), which was probably the capital of Goshen, and, by direction of Moses, the place of general rendezvous previous to their departure. <div eID="gen2156" type="x-p"/>
entries.89273fa67c739bfead0906be67cd769b32186ec0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1608"/><div sID="gen2157" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1608"/><hi type="bold">4. upon their gods--</hi>used either according to Scripture phraseology to denote their rulers (the first-born of the king and his princes) or the idolatrous objects of Egyptian worship. <div eID="gen2157" type="x-p"/>

Marah--</hi>thought to be Ain Howarah, both from its position and the time (three days) it would take them with their children and flocks to march from the water of Ayun Musa to that spot. <div eID="gen2161" type="x-p"/>
entries.30bbe25d1a28446f0da99c4db33235b5c68f40a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1613"/><div sID="gen2162" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1613"/><hi type="bold">9. Elim--</hi>supposed to be Wady Ghurundel (see on <reference osisRef="Exod.15.27">Ex 15:27</reference>). <div eID="gen2162" type="x-p"/>
entries.334962757958c760a185d41c82dd01b5e4e78998: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1614"/><div sID="gen2163" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1614"/><hi type="bold">10. encamped by the Red Sea--</hi>The road from Wady Ghurundel leads into the interior, in consequence of a high continuous ridge which excludes all view of the sea. At the mouth of Wady-et-Tayibeh, after about three days' march, it opens again on a plain along the margin of the Red Sea. The minute accuracy of the Scripture narrative, in corresponding so exactly with the geographical features of this region, is remarkably shown in describing the Israelites as proceeding by the only practicable route that could be taken. This plain, where they encamped, was the Desert of Sin (see on <reference osisRef="Exod.16.1">Ex 16:1</reference>). <div eID="gen2163" type="x-p"/>
entries.18d80912ee72b6cbd316bcad91fa0799ef6b0ad2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1615"/><div sID="gen2164" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1615"/><hi type="bold">12-14. Dophkah ... Alush ... Rephidim--</hi>These three stations, in the great valleys of El Sheikh and Feiran, would be equivalent to four days' journey for such a host. Rephidim (<reference osisRef="Exod.17.6">Ex 17:6</reference>) was in Horeb, the burnt region--a generic name for a hot, mountainous country. [See on <reference osisRef="Exod.17.1">Ex 17:1</reference>.] <div eID="gen2164" type="x-p"/>

entries.092dfecbc186062785f01aa888f8d54f3e343046: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1617"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Num.33.16-Num.33.56">Nu 33:16-56</reference>. From Sinai to Kadesh and Plains of Moab.</title> <div sID="gen2166" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1617"/><hi type="bold">16-37. Kibroth-Hattaavah ("the graves of lust," see on <reference osisRef="Num.11.34">Nu 11:34</reference>)--</hi>The route, on breaking up the encampment at Sinai, led down Wady Sheikh; then crossing Jebel-et-Tih, which intersected the peninsula, they descended into Wady Zalaka, pitching successively at two brief, though memorable, stations (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.22">De 9:22</reference>); then they encamped at Hazeroth ("unwalled villages"), supposed to be at Ain-Hadera (see on <reference osisRef="Num.11.35">Nu 11:35</reference>). Kadesh, or Kadesh-barnea, is supposed to be the great valley of the Ghor, and the city Kadesh to have been situated on the border of this valley [Burckhardt; Robinson]. But as there are no less than eighteen stations inserted between Hazeroth and Kadesh, and only eleven days were spent in performing that journey (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.2">De 1:2</reference>), it is evident that the intermediate stations here recorded belong to another and totally different visit to Kadesh. The first was when they left Sinai in the second month (<reference osisRef="Num.1.11">Nu 1:11</reference>; 13:20), and were in Kadesh in August (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.45">De 1:45</reference>), and "abode many days" in it. Then, murmuring at the report of the spies, they were commanded to return into the desert "by the way of the Red Sea." The arrival at Kadesh, mentioned in this catalogue, corresponds to the second sojourn at that place, being the first month, or April (<reference osisRef="Num.20.1">Nu 20:1</reference>). Between the two visits there intervened a period of thirty-eight years, during which they wandered hither and thither through all the region of El-Tih ("wanderings"), often returning to the same spots as the pastoral necessities of their flocks required; and there is the strongest reason for believing that the stations named between Hazeroth (<reference osisRef="Num.33.8">Nu 33:8</reference>) and Kadesh (<reference osisRef="Num.33.36">Nu 33:36</reference>) belong to the long interval of wandering. No certainty has yet been attained in ascertaining the locale of many of these stations. There must have been more than are recorded; for it is probable that those only are noted where they remained some time, where the tabernacle was pitched, and where Moses and the elders encamped, the people being scattered for pasture in various directions. From Ezion-geber, for instance, which stood at the head of the gulf of Akaba, to Kadesh, could not be much less than the whole length of the great valley of the Ghor, a distance of not less than a hundred miles, whatever might be the exact situation of Kadesh; and, of course, there must have been several intervening stations, though none are mentioned. The incidents and stages of the rest of the journey to the plains of Moab are sufficiently explicit from the preceding chapters. <div eID="gen2166" type="x-p"/>
entries.925da34a671d4f65dd10cd283071cbf358352e1a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1620"/><div sID="gen2169" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1620"/><hi type="bold">50-53. ye shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you--</hi>not, however, by expulsion, but extermination (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.1">De 7:1</reference>).<div eID="gen2169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2170" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and destroy all their pictures--</hi>obelisks for idolatrous worship (see on <reference osisRef="Lev.26.1">Le 26:1</reference>).<div eID="gen2170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2171" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and destroy all their molten images, and quite pluck down all their high places--</hi>by metonymy for all their groves and altars, and materials of worship on the tops of hills. <div eID="gen2171" type="x-p"/>
entries.d276e36ae1aded9e38608e742c020ed6a474800a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1621"/><div sID="gen2172" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1621"/><hi type="bold">54. ye shall divide the land by lot--</hi>The particular locality of each tribe was to be determined in this manner while a line was to be used in measuring the proportion (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.10">Jos 18:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.16.5">Psa 16:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.6">6</reference>). <div eID="gen2172" type="x-p"/>
entries.9de5d48d69380a28a4126769788cced41ce15bf4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1622"/><div sID="gen2173" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1622"/><hi type="bold">55. But if ye will not drive out the inhabitants of the land from before you--</hi>No associations were to be formed with the inhabitants; otherwise, "if ye let remain, they will be pricks in your eyes, and thorns in your sides"--that is, they would prove troublesome and dangerous neighbors, enticing to idolatry, and consequently depriving you of the divine favor and blessing. The neglect of the counsel against union with the idolatrous inhabitants became fatal to them. This earnest admonition given to the Israelites in their peculiar circumstances conveys a salutary lesson to us to allow no lurking habits of sin to remain in us. That spiritual enemy must be eradicated from our nature; otherwise it will be ruinous to our present peace and future salvation. <chapter eID="Num.33"/>

entries.c200efbc981500ba8a798e987b510c0ef70b62f7: <div eID="gen6184" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen6185" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6186" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6186" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6185" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6187" type="x-p"/> The journeyings of the Israelites written out by Moses, according to the commandment of the Lord, <reference osisRef="Num.33.1">Num 33:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.33.2">Num 33:2</reference>. They depart from Rameses on the fifteenth day of the first month, on the day after the passover, the first-born of the Egyptians having been slain, <reference osisRef="Num.33.3">Num 33:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.33.4">Num 33:4</reference>. Their forty-two stations enumerated, vv. 5-49. They are authorized to expel all the former inhabitants, and destroy all remnants of idolatry, <reference osisRef="Num.33.50-Num.33.53">Num 33:50-53</reference>. The land is to be divided by lot, <reference osisRef="Num.33.54">Num 33:54</reference>. Should they not drive out the former inhabitants, they shall be to them as pricks in their eyes and thorns in their sides, <reference osisRef="Num.33.55">Num 33:55</reference>. And if not obedient, God will deal with them as he has purposed to do with the Canaanites, <reference osisRef="Num.33.56">Num 33:56</reference>.
entries.c1ed2203bd9d60458176bddd2487d862b953ec9e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen6187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6188" type="x-p"/> And Moses wrote their goings out according to their journeys - We may consider the whole book of Numbers as a diary, and indeed the first book of travels ever published. Dr. Shaw, Dr. Pococke, and several others, have endeavored to mark out the route of the Israelites, through this great, dreary, and trackless desert, and have ascertained many of the stages here described. Indeed there are sufficient evidences of this important journey still remaining, for the descriptions of many are so particular that the places are readily ascertained by them; but this is not the case with all. Israel was the Church of God in the wilderness, and its unsettled, wandering state under Moses may point out the unsettled state of religion under the law. Their being brought, after the death of Moses, into the promised rest by Joshua, may point out the establishment, fixedness, and certainty of that salvation provided by Jesus Christ, of whom Joshua, in name and conduct, was a remarkable type. Mr. Ainsworth imagines that the forty-two stations here enumerated, through which the Israelites were brought to the verge of the promised land, and afterwards taken over Jordan into the rest which God had promised, point out the forty-two generations from Abraham unto Christ, through whom the Savior of the world came, by whose blood we have an entrance into the holiest, and enjoy the inheritance among the saints in light. And Mr. Bromley, in his Way to the Sabbath of Rest, considers each name and place as descriptive of the spiritual state through which a soul passes in its way to the kingdom of God. But in cases of this kind fancy has much more to do than judgment.
entries.c7b5e826fd58b2c045797ab17cd7a90c2349f887: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen6188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6189" type="x-p"/> From Rameses - This appears to have been the metropolis of the land of Goshen, and the place of rendezvous whence the whole Israelitish nation set out on their journey to the promised land; and is supposed to be the same as Cairo. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Exo.12.37">Exo 12:37</reference>. <div eID="gen6189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6190" type="x-p"/> Here Follow the Forty-Two Stations <div eID="gen6190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6191" type="x-p"/> Station 1.
entries.fd67d6697ae2be1b9040d79ddd2718942d1915ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen6191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6192" type="x-p"/> And pitched in Succoth - This name signifies booths or tents, and probably refers to no town or village, but simply designates the place where they pitched their tents for the first time after their departure from Rameses. <div eID="gen6192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6193" type="x-p"/> Stat. 2.
entries.1eb39664f0d29705f6234dbc95393858f3b0f142: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen6193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6194" type="x-p"/> Etham, which is in the edge of the wilderness - This place is not well known; Dr. Shaw supposes it to have been one mile from Cairo. Calmet thinks it is the city of Buthum mentioned by Herodotus, which he places in Arabia, on the frontiers of Egypt. <div eID="gen6194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6195" type="x-p"/> Stat. 3.
entries.c3f23a89d6ba7a88cd3e9a3048c8236d1d59ae57: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen6195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6196" type="x-p"/> Pi-hahiroth - See on <reference osisRef="Exo.14.1">Exo 14:1</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Exo.14.2">Exo 14:2</reference> (note). Baal-zephon Calmet supposes to be the Clysma of the Greeks, and the Kolzum of the Arabians. <div eID="gen6196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6197" type="x-p"/> Stat. 4.
entries.975e5c06661c2eac67b56a321108ba2f798c9e2d: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen6197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6198" type="x-p"/> And went three days' journey in the wilderness of Etham - Called the wilderness of Shur, <reference osisRef="Exo.15.22">Exo 15:22</reference>. <div eID="gen6198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6199" type="x-p"/> And pitched in Marah - Dr. Shaw supposes this place to be at Sedur, over against the valley of Baideah, on the opposite side of the Red Sea. <div eID="gen6199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6200" type="x-p"/> Stat. 5.
entries.15e48d14b3a3c264a937c3694c9ed11a28c47817: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen6200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6201" type="x-p"/> And came unto Elim - A place on the skirts of the deserts of Sin, two leagues from Tor, and nearly thirty from Corondel, a large bay on the east side of the Red Sea. Dr. Shaw, when he visited this place, found but nine of the twelve wells mentioned in the text, and instead of 70 palm trees, he found upwards of 2,000. See on <reference osisRef="Exo.15.27">Exo 15:27</reference> (note). <div eID="gen6201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6202" type="x-p"/> Stat. 6.
entries.39cd0628a145802186a2d8691ba760e8d824487a: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen6202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6203" type="x-p"/> Encamped by the Red Sea - It is difficult to assign the place of this encampment, as the Israelites were now on their way to Mount Sinai, which lay considerably to the east of Elim, and consequently farther from the sea than the former station. It might be called by the Red Sea, as the Israelites had it, as the principal object, still in view. This station however is mentioned nowhere else. By the Red Sea we are not to understand a sea, the waters of which are red, or the sand red, or any thing else about or in it red; for nothing of this kind appears. It is called in Hebrew ים סוף yam suph, which signifies the weedy sea. The Septuagint rendered the original by θαλασσα εραθρα, and the Vulgate after it by mare rubrum, and the European versions followed these, and, in opposition to etymology and reason, translated it the Red Sea. See the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.10.19">Exo 10:19</reference>. <div eID="gen6203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6204" type="x-p"/> Stat. 7.

entries.4c4fc29846bbc68e3e1393a3afac2002aead81f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen6210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6211" type="x-p"/> Rephidim - Remarkable for the rebellion of the Israelites against Moses, because of the want of water, Exodus 17. <div eID="gen6211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6212" type="x-p"/> Stat. 11.
entries.e2b61c4a6aa53dfe2878bfff12ac756461d889fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen6212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6213" type="x-p"/> The wilderness of Sinai - Somewhere northward of Mount Sinai, on the straight road to the promised land, to which they now directed their course. <div eID="gen6213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6214" type="x-p"/> Stat. 12.
entries.342f0fadadc81268810751366fac5325d6b85831: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen6214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6215" type="x-p"/> Kibroth-hattaavah - No city, village, etc., but a place in the open desert, which had its name from the plague that fell upon the Israelites, through their murmuring against God, and their inordinate desire of flesh. See on Numbers 11 (note). But it appears that the Israelites had traveled three days' journey in order to reach this place, <reference osisRef="Num.10.33">Num 10:33</reference>, and commentators suppose there must have been other stations which are not laid down here, probably because the places were not remarkable. <div eID="gen6215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6216" type="x-p"/> Stat. 13.

entries.a3b8fcd459b028e67d3187e3f13c35139db1b4f5: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen6218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6219" type="x-p"/> Rithmah - This place lay somewhere in the wilderness of Paran, through which the Israelites were now passing. entries.1c9912ebc06d7c4da8cf1f52297bc2b5e3eb1a8b: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen6230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6231" type="x-p"/> Haradah - Unknown, Calmet supposes that it may be the place called Bered, <reference osisRef="Gen.16.14">Gen 16:14</reference>, which was in the vicinity of Kadesh. <div eID="gen6231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6232" type="x-p"/> Stat. 21.
entries.4b6129195096c330d6c2c8d6d1d61ae33f3de5fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen6232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6233" type="x-p"/> Makheloth - A name found nowhere else in Scripture. <div eID="gen6233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6234" type="x-p"/> Stat. 22.
entries.b9b95100b394887397bbe3a096b2cf7bdf0f177e: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen6234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6235" type="x-p"/> Tahath - Unknown. <div eID="gen6235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6236" type="x-p"/> Stat. 23.

entries.d968e4cd10ae68135c7fda7c943b79fdae2f19e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen6238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6239" type="x-p"/> Mithcah - Calmet conjectures that this may be Mocha, a city in Arabia Petraea. <div eID="gen6239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6240" type="x-p"/> Stat. 25.
entries.4f07f7a34d6087ed9aee06cef52d56c5070da6d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen6240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6241" type="x-p"/> Hashmonah - Supposed by some to be the same as Azmon, <reference osisRef="Num.34.4">Num 34:4</reference>. <div eID="gen6241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6242" type="x-p"/> Stat. 26.
entries.cbd14e52cf254eaad04f567e2e80ea23fa95ed3d: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen6242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6243" type="x-p"/> Moseroth - Situation unknown. In <reference osisRef="Deu.10.6">Deu 10:6</reference> it is said that the Israelites took their journey from Beeroth, the wells of the children of Jaakan, to Mosera, and there Aaron died. If so, Mosera, Moseroth, and Hor, must be different names of the same place; or Moseroth, or Mosera, must have been some town or village near Mount Hor, for there Aaron died. See <reference osisRef="Num.33.38">Num 33:38</reference>. <div eID="gen6243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6244" type="x-p"/> Stat. 27.
entries.ff15e06806bae74e23639471a962a59ce0c913f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen6244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6245" type="x-p"/> Bene-jaakan - Unknown. The sons of Jaakan. entries.71b86832d1f5a9a3fb45411094f3d3321b682b7b: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen6246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6247" type="x-p"/> Hor-hagidgad - The hole or pit of Gidgad. Unknown. entries.8ded87f534f86a4a72d220a7966c7de821d53dd9: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen6251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6252" type="x-p"/> Ezion-gaber - Dr. Shaw places this port on the western coast of the Elantic gulf of the Red Sea. It is now called Meenah el Dsahab, or the golden port, by the Arabs; because it was from this place that Solomon sent his ships for gold to Ophir, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.26">1Kgs 9:26</reference>. He supposes it to be about sixty miles distant from Mount Sinai - Travels, p. 322, 4th. edition. <div eID="gen6252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6253" type="x-p"/> Stat. 32.
entries.aa48e43f313ec55abfd992d9fb819ab97d11672b: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen6253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6254" type="x-p"/> Zin, which is Kadesh - A place remarkable for the death of Miriam the prophetess, and bringing water out of the rock. As this place was on the borders of Edom, the Israelites, being denied permission to pass through their land, which lay on the direct road to the promised land, were obliged to turn to the right to Mount Hor, now called Accaba by the Arabs. <div eID="gen6254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6255" type="x-p"/> Stat. 33.
entries.d15fbfd8ad84faeb8110420a9da80e9eab0b7fe4: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen6255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6256" type="x-p"/> Hor - Famous for the death of Aaron. See on Numbers 20 (note). Perhaps Moseroth or Mosera, <reference osisRef="Num.33.30">Num 33:30</reference> (note), was a village near this mountain. <div eID="gen6256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6257" type="x-p"/> Stat. 34.
entries.8466782e15b5203f730b788c4869509a61a5b65d: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen6257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6258" type="x-p"/> Zalmonah - Probably in the neighborhood of the land of Edom. entries.4033f11b3736904bad2e5de28592747bc269325e: <hi type="bold">Verse 52</hi> <div eID="gen6275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6276" type="x-p"/> Ye shall - destroy all their pictures - משכיתם maskiyotham, from שחה sachah, to be like, or resemble, either pictures, carved work, or embroidery, as far as these things were employed to exhibit the abominations of idolatry. entries.8739c01f63122cedc39b4c947f54f18cf036c34a: <hi type="bold">Verse 55</hi> <div eID="gen6276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6277" type="x-p"/> Shall be pricks in your eyes - Under these metaphors, the continual mischief that should be done to them, both in soul and body, by these idolaters, is set forth in a very expressive manner. What can be more vexatious than a continual goading of each side, so that the attempt to avoid the one throws the body more forcibly on the other? And what can be more distressing than a continual pricking in the eye, harassing the mind, tormenting the body, and extinguishing the sight? <div eID="gen6277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6278" type="x-p"/> 1. It has been usual among pious men to consider these Canaanites remaining in the land, as emblems of indwelling sin; and it must be granted that what those remaining Canaanites were to the people of Israel, who were disobedient to God, such is indwelling sin to all those who will not have the blood of the covenant to cleanse them from all unrighteousness. For a time, while conscience is tender, such persons feel themselves straitened in all their goings, hindered in all their religious services, and distressed beyond measure because of the law - the authority and power of sin, which they find warring in their members: by and by the eye of their mind becomes obscured by the constant piercings of sin, till at last, fatally persuaded that sin must dwell in them as long as they live, they accommodate their minds to their situation, their consciences cease to be tender, and they content themselves with expecting redemption where and when it has never been promised, viz., beyond the grave! On the subject of the journeyings of the Israelites, the following observations from old Mr. Ainsworth cannot fail to interest the reader. <div eID="gen6278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6279" type="x-p"/> 2. "The Travels of Israel through that great and terrible wilderness, wherein were fiery serpents, and scorpions, and drought, where there was no water, <reference osisRef="Deu.8.15">Deu 8:15</reference>, which was a land of deserts, and of pits, a land of drought, and of the shadow of death, a land that no man passed through, and where no man dwelt, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.6">Jer 2:6</reference>, signified the many troubles and afflictions through which we must enter into the kingdom of God, <reference osisRef="Act.14.22">Act 14:22</reference>. The helps, comforts, and deliverances which God gave unto his people in their distresses, are examples of his love and mercy towards his followers; for he comforts them in all their tribulation, that as the sufferings of Christ abound in them, so their consolation also abounds in Christ, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.5">2Cor 1:5</reference>. The punishments which God inflicted upon the disobedient, who perished in the wilderness for their sins, happened unto them for ensamples, and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.1">1Cor 10:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.11">1Cor 10:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.3.17">Heb 3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.18">Heb 3:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.19">Heb 3:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.1">Heb 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.2">Heb 4:2</reference>. By the names of their encamping places, and histories adjoined, it appears how Israel came sometimes into straits and troublesome ways, as at Pihahiroth, <reference osisRef="Exo.14.2">Exo 14:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.14.3">Exo 14:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.14.10">Exo 14:10</reference>, etc.; and at Zalmonah, <reference osisRef="Num.2.1">Num 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.2.4">Num 2:4</reference>, etc.; sometimes into large and ample room, as at the plains of Moab; sometimes to places of hunger and thirst, as at Rephidim and Kadesh, Exodus 16, 17; Numbers 20; sometimes to places of refreshing, as at Elim and Beer, <reference osisRef="Exo.15.27">Exo 15:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.21.16">Num 21:16</reference>; sometimes where they had wars, as at Rephidim, Kadesh, Edrei, <reference osisRef="Exo.17.8">Exo 17:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.21.1">Num 21:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.21.33">Num 21:33</reference>; sometimes where they had rest, as at Mount Sinai: sometimes they went right forward, as from Sinai to Kadesh-barnea; sometimes they turned backward, as from Kadesh-barnea to the Red Sea: sometimes they came to mountains, as Sinai, Shapher, Hor-Gidgad; sometimes to valleys, as Tahath, etc.; sometimes to places of bitterness, as Marah; sometimes, of sweetness, as Mithcah. <div eID="gen6279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6280" type="x-p"/> 3. "The Sins which they committed in the wilderness were many and great; as open Idolatry by the calf, at Horeb, Exodus 32, and with Baal-peor, Numbers 25. Unbelief, at Kadesh, Numbers 14; and afterwards Presumptuous Boldness in the same place; Murmuring against God sundry times, with tempting of Christ, (as the apostle speaks, 1 Corinthians 15). Contention and Rebellion against their governors often; lusting for flesh to fill their appetites, and loathing manna, the heavenly food; Whoredom with the daughters of Moab, and many other provocations; so that this complaint is after made of them, How oft did they provoke him in the wilderness, and grieve him in the desert! <reference osisRef="Psa.78.40">Psa 78:40</reference>. All sorts of persons sinned against God; the multitude of people very often; the mixed multitude of strangers among them, Numbers 11. The princes, as the ten spies, Dathan, Abiram, etc. The Levites, as Korah and his company; Miriam the prophetess, Numbers 12; Aaron the priest with her, besides his sin at Horeb, Exodus 32; and at the water of Meribah, Numbers 20. Moses also himself at the same place, for which he was excluded from the land of Canaan. <div eID="gen6280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6281" type="x-p"/> 4. "The Punishments laid on them by the Lord for their disobedience were many. They died by the sword of the enemy, as of the Amalekites, Exodus 17, and of the Canaanites, <reference osisRef="Num.14.45">Num 14:45</reference>; and some by the sword of their brethren, Exodus 32. Some were burned with fire, Numbers 11, 16; some died with surfeit, Numbers 11; some were swallowed up alive in the earth, Numbers 16; some were killed with serpents, Numbers 21; many died of the pestilence, <reference osisRef="Num.16.46">Num 16:46</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Num.5.25">Num 5:25</reference>; and generally all that generation which were first mustered, after their coming out of Egypt, perished, <reference osisRef="Num.26.64">Num 26:64</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.26.65">Num 26:65</reference>. God consumed their days in vanity, and their years in terror, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.33">Psa 78:33</reference>. <div eID="gen6281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6282" type="x-p"/> 5. "Nevertheless, for his name's sake, he magnified his Mercies unto them and their posterity. He had divided the sea, and led them through on dry land, drowning their enemies, Exodus 14. He led them with a cloud by day, and a pillar of fire by night, continually. He gave them manna from heaven daily. He clave the rock, and gave them water for their thirst. He fed them with quails, when they longed for flesh. He sweetened the bitter waters. He saved them from the sword of their enemies. He delivered them from the fiery serpents and scorpions. Their raiment waxed not old upon them, neither did their foot swell for forty years, <reference osisRef="Deu.8.4">Deu 8:4</reference>. He delivered them from the intended curse of Balaam, and turned it into a blessing, because he loved them, Numbers 22; <reference osisRef="Deu.23.5">Deu 23:5</reference>. He came down from Mount Sinai, and spake with them from heaven, and gave them right judgments and true laws, good statutes and commandments, and gave also his good Spirit to instruct them, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.13">Neh 9:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.20">Neh 9:20</reference>. In the times of his wrath he remembered mercy; his eye spared them from destroying them, neither did he make an end of them in the wilderness, <reference osisRef="Eze.20.17">Eze 20:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.20.22">Eze 20:22</reference>. He gave them kingdoms and nations, and they possessed the lands of their enemies; and he multiplied their children as the stars of heaven, and brought them into the land promised unto their forefathers. <reference osisRef="Neh.9.22">Neh 9:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.23">Neh 9:23</reference>. Now whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we, through patience and comfort of the Scriptures, might have hope, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.4">Rom 15:4</reference>." Let him that readeth understand."  <chapter eID="Num.33"/> <div eID="gen6282" type="x-p"/>

entries.805c32e399b467f100355dca9e245a3a12e9a5a1: Num 33:1-15 <div eID="gen2062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2063" type="x-p"/> The first and second verses form the heading: “<hi type="italic">These are the marches of the children of Israel, which they marched out,</hi>” i.e., the marches which they made from one place to another, on going out of Egypt. מסּע does not mean a station, but the breaking up of a camp, and then a train, or march (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.12.37">Exo 12:37</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Gen.13.3">Gen 13:3</reference>). לצבאתם (see <reference osisRef="Exod.7.4">Exo 7:4</reference>). בּיד, under the guidance, as in Num 4:28, and Exo 38:21. למסעיהם מוצאיהם, “<hi type="italic">their goings out</hi> (properly, their places of departure) <hi type="italic">according to their marches</hi>,” is really equivalent to the clause which follows: “<hi type="italic">their marches according to their places of departure</hi>.” The march of the people is not described by the stations, or places of encampment, but by the particular spots from which they set out. Hence the constant repetition of the word ויּסעוּ, “<hi type="italic">and they broke up</hi>.” In Num 33:3-5, the departure is described according to <reference osisRef="Exod.12.17">Exo 12:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.37">Exo 12:37</reference>-41. On the judgments of Jehovah upon the gods of Egypt, see at Exo 12:12. “With an high hand:” as in Exo 14:8. - The places of encampment from <hi type="italic">Succoth</hi> to the <hi type="italic">desert of Sinai</hi> (Num 33:5-15) agree with those in the historical account, except that the stations at the <hi type="italic">Red</hi> <hi type="italic">Sea</hi> (Num 33:10) and those at <hi type="italic">Dophkah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Alush</hi> (Num 33:13 and Num 33:14) are passed over there. For <hi type="italic">Raemses</hi>, see at Exo 12:37. <hi type="italic">Succoth</hi> and <hi type="italic">Etham</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.20">Exo 13:20</reference>). <hi type="italic">Pihahiroth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.2">Exo 14:2</reference>). “<hi type="italic">The</hi> <hi type="italic">wilderness</hi>” (Num 33:8) is the desert of <hi type="italic">Shur</hi>, according to Exo 15:22. <hi type="italic">Marah</hi>, see Exo 15:23. <hi type="italic">Elim</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.27">Exo 15:27</reference>). For the <hi type="italic">Red Sea</hi> and the <hi type="italic">wilderness of Sin</hi>, see Exo 16:1. For <hi type="italic">Dophkah</hi>, <hi type="italic">Alush</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Rephidim</hi>, see <reference osisRef="Exod.17.1">Exo 17:1</reference>; and for the wilderness of <hi type="italic">Sinai</hi>, Exo 19:2.
entries.79671b3aa2c2c56a27ba6210f421d68d54bef23d: Numbers 33:16-35 <div eID="gen2063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2064" type="x-p"/> In vv. 16-36 there follow twenty-one names of places where the Israelites encamped from the time that they left the <hi type="italic">wilderness of Sinai</hi> till they encamped in the <hi type="italic">wilderness of Zin</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">Kadesh</hi>. The description of the latter as “the wilderness of Zin, which is Kadesh,” which agrees almost word for word with Num 20:1, and still more the agreement of the places mentioned in Num 33:37-49, as the encampments of Israel after leaving Kadesh till their arrival in the steppes of Moab, with the march of the people in the fortieth year as described in Num 20:22-22:1, put it beyond all doubt that the encampment in the wilderness of Zin, i.e., Kadesh (Num 33:36), is to be understood as referring to the second arrival in Kadesh after the expiration of the thirty-eight years of wandering in the desert to which the congregation had been condemned. Consequently the twenty-one names in vv. 16-36 contain not only the places of encampment at which the Israelites encamped in the second year of their march from Sinai to the desert of <hi type="italic">Paran</hi> at Kadesh, whence the spies were despatched into Canaan, but also those in which they encamped for a longer period during the thirty-eight years of punishment in the wilderness. This view is still further confirmed by the fact that the two first of the stations named after the departure from the wilderness of Sinai, viz., <hi type="italic">Kibroth-hattaavah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Hazeroth</hi>, agree with those named in the historical account in Num 11:34 and Num 11:35. Now if, according to Num 12:16, when the people left <hi type="italic">Hazeroth</hi>, they encamped in the desert of <hi type="italic">Paran</hi>, and despatched the spies thence out of the desert of <hi type="italic">Zin</hi> (Num 13:21), who returned to the congregation after forty days “into the desert of Paran to <hi type="italic">Kadesh</hi>” (Num 13:26), it is as natural as it well can be to seek for this place of encampment in the desert of Paran or Zin at Kadesh under the name of <hi type="italic">Rithmah</hi>, which follows Hazeroth in the present list (Num 33:18). This natural supposition reaches the highest degree of probability, from the fact that, in the historical account, the place of encampment, from which the sending out of the spies took place, is described in so indefinite a manner as the “desert of <hi type="italic">Paran</hi>,” since this name does not belong to a small desert, just capable of holding the camp of the Israelites, but embraces the whole of the large desert plateau which stretches from the central mountains of Horeb in the south to the mountains of the Amorites, which really form part of Canaan, and contains no less than 400 (? 10,000 English) square miles. In this desert the Israelites could only pitch their camp in one particular spot, which is called <hi type="italic">Rithmah</hi> in the list before us; whereas in the historical account the passage is described, according to what the Israelites performed and experienced in this encampment, as near to the southern border of Canaan, and is thus pointed out with sufficient clearness for the purpose of the historical account. To this we may add the coincidence of the name <hi type="italic">Rithmah</hi> with the Wady <hi type="italic">Abu Retemat</hi>, which is not very far to the south of Kadesh, “a wide plain with shrubs and <hi type="italic">retem</hi>,” i.e., broom (Robinson, i. p. 279), in the neighbourhood of which, and behind the chalk formation which bounds it towards the east, there is a copious spring of sweet water called <hi type="italic">Ain el Kudeirât</hi>. This spot was well adapted for a place of encampment for Israel, which was so numerous that it might easily stretch into the desert of Zin, and as far as Kadesh. <div eID="gen2064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2065" type="x-p"/> The seventeen places of encampment, therefore, that are mentioned in vv. 19-36 between <hi type="italic">Rithmah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Kadesh</hi>, are the places at which Israel set up in the desert, from their return from Kadesh into the “desert of the way to the Red Sea” (Num 14:25), till the reassembling of the whole congregation in the desert of Zin at Kadesh (Num 20:1).<note placement="foot">The different hypotheses for reducing the journey of the Israelites to a few years, have been refuted by <hi type="italic">Kurtz</hi> (iii. §41) in the most conclusive manner possible, and in some respects more elaborately than was actually necessary. Nevertheless <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> has made a fresh attempt, in the interest of his fragmentary hypothesis, to explain the twenty-one places of encampment given in vv. 16-37 as twenty-one marches made by Israel from Sinai till their first arrival at Kadesh. As the whole distance from Sinai to Kadesh by the straight road through the desert consists of only an eleven days’ journey,<hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> endeavours to bring his twenty-one marches into harmony with this statement, by reckoning only five hours to each march, and postulating a few detours in addition, in which the people occupied about a hundred hours or more. The objection which might be raised to this, namely, that the Israelites made much longer marches than these on their way from Egypt to Sinai, he tries to set aside by supposing that the Israelites left their flocks behind them in Egypt, and procured fresh ones from the Bedouins at Sinai. But this assertion is so arbitrary and baseless an idea, that it is not worth while to waste a single word upon the subject (see <reference osisRef="Exod.12.38">Exo 12:38</reference>). The reduction of the places of encampment to simple marches is proved to be at variance with the text by the express statement in Num 10:33, that when the Israelites left the wilderness of Sinai they went a three days’ journey, until the cloud showed them a resting-place. For it is perfectly evydent from this, that the march from one place to another cannot be understood without further ground as being simply a day’s march of five hours.</note> <div eID="gen2065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2066" type="x-p"/> Of all the seventeen places not a single one is known, or can be pointed out with certainty, except <hi type="italic">Eziongeber</hi>. Only the four mentioned in Num 33:30-33, <hi type="italic">Moseroth</hi>, <hi type="italic">Bene-Jaakan</hi>, <hi type="italic">Hor-hagidgad</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Jotbathah</hi>, are referred to again, viz., in <reference osisRef="Deut.10.6-Deut.10.7">Deu 10:6-7</reference>, where Moses refers to the divine protection enjoyed by the Israelites in their wandering in the desert, in these words: “And the children of Israel took their journey from <hi type="italic">Beeroth-bene-Jaakan</hi> to <hi type="italic">Mosera</hi>; there Aaron died, and there he was buried.... From thence they journeyed unto <hi type="italic">Gudgodah</hi>, and from <hi type="italic">Gudgodah</hi> to <hi type="italic">Jotbathah</hi>, a land of water-brooks.” Of the identity of the places mentioned in the two passages there can be no doubt whatever. <hi type="italic">Bene Jaakan</hi> is simply an abbreviation of <hi type="italic">Beeroth-bene-Jaakan</hi>, wells of the children of Jaakan. Now if the children of <hi type="italic">Jaakan</hi> were the same as the Horite family of <hi type="italic">Kanan</hi> mentioned in <reference osisRef="Gen.36.27">Gen 36:27</reference>, - and the reading יעקן for ועקן in <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.42">1Ch 1:42</reference> seems to favour this-the wells of <hi type="italic">Jaakan</hi> would have to be sought for on the mountains that bound the <hi type="italic">Arabah</hi> on either the east or west.<hi type="italic">Gudgodah</hi> is only a slightly altered and abbreviated form of <hi type="italic">Hor-hagidgad</hi>, the cave of <hi type="italic">Gidgad</hi> or <hi type="italic">Gudgodah</hi>; and lastly, <hi type="italic">Moseroth</hi> is simply the plural form of <hi type="italic">Mosera</hi>. But notwithstanding the identity of these four places, the two passages relate to different journeys. <reference osisRef="Deut.10.6">Deu 10:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.10.7">Deu 10:7</reference> refers to the march in the fortieth year, when the Israelites went from Kadesh through the Wady <hi type="italic">Murreh</hi> into the Arabah to Mount <hi type="italic">Hor</hi>, and encamped in the Arabah first of all at the wells of the children, and then at <hi type="italic">Mosera</hi>, where Aaron died upon Mount <hi type="italic">Hor</hi>, which was in the neighbourhood, and whence they travelled still farther southwards to <hi type="italic">Gudgodah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jotbathah</hi>. In the historical account in Num 20 and 21 the three places of encampment, <hi type="italic">Bene-Jaakan</hi>, <hi type="italic">Gudgodah</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Jotbathah</hi>, are not mentioned, because nothing worthy of note occurred there. <hi type="italic">Gudgodah</hi> was perhaps the place of encampment mentioned in Num 21:4, the name of which is not given, where the people were punished with fiery serpents; and <hi type="italic">Jotbathah</hi> is probably to be placed before <hi type="italic">Zalmonah</hi> (Num 33:41). The clause, “a land of water-brooks” (<reference osisRef="Deut.10.7">Deu 10:7</reference>), points to a spot in or near the southern part of the Arabah, where some wady, or valley with a stream flowing through it, opened into the Arabah from either the eastern or western mountains, and formed a green oasis through its copious supply of water in the midst of the arid steppe. But the Israelites had encamped at the very same places once before, namely, during their thirty-seven years of wandering, in which the people, after returning from Kadesh to the Red Sea through the centre of the great desert of <hi type="italic">et Tih</hi>, after wandering about for some time in the broad desert plateau, went through the Wady <hi type="italic">el Jerafeh</hi> into the Arabah as far as the eastern border of it on the slopes of Mount Hor, and there encamped at <hi type="italic">Mosera</hi> (<hi type="italic">Moseroth</hi>) somewhere near <hi type="italic">Ain et Taiyibeh</hi> (on Robinson<hi type="italic">'s</hi> map), and then crossed over to <hi type="italic">Bene-Jaakan</hi>, which was probably on the western border of the Arabah, somewhere near <hi type="italic">Ain el Ghamr</hi> (Robinson), and then turning southwards passed along the Wady <hi type="italic">el</hi> <hi type="italic">Jeib</hi> by <hi type="italic">Hor-gidgad</hi> (<hi type="italic">Gudgodah</hi>), <hi type="italic">Jotbathah</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Abronah</hi> to <hi type="italic">Eziongeber</hi> on the Red Sea; for there can be no doubt whatever that the <hi type="italic">Eziongeber</hi> in Num 33:35, Num 33:36, and that in <reference osisRef="Deut.2.8">Deu 2:8</reference>, are one and the same town, viz., the well-known port at the northern extremity of the Elanitic Gulf, where the Israelites in the time of Solomon and Jehoshaphat built a fleet to sail to <hi type="italic">Ophir</hi> (1Ki 9:26; 1Ki 22:49). It was not far from <hi type="italic">Elath</hi> (i.e., <hi type="italic">Akaba</hi>), and is supposed to have been “the large and beautiful town of <hi type="italic">Asziun</hi>,” which formerly stood, according to <hi type="italic">Makrizi</hi>, near to <hi type="italic">Aila</hi>, where there were many dates, fields, and fruit-trees, though it has now long since entirely disappeared. <div eID="gen2066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2067" type="x-p"/> Consequently the Israelites passed twice through a portion of the Arabah in a southerly direction towards the Red Sea, the second time from Wady Murreh by Mount Hor, to go round the land of Edom, not quite to the head of the gulf, but only to the Wady <hi type="italic">el Ithm</hi>, through which they crossed to the eastern side of Edomitis; the first time during the thirty-seven years of wandering from Wady el Jerafeh to Moseroth and Bene Jaakan, and thence to Eziongeber.
entries.2ac639b66209e62ca430cdbc5cbf48e8f7824c29: Num 33:36 <div eID="gen2067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2068" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And they removed from Eziongeber, and encamped in the desert of Zin, that is Kadesh:</hi>” the return to Kadesh towards the end of the thirty-ninth year is referred to here. The fact that no places of encampment are given between Eziongeber and Kadesh, is not to be attributed to the “plan of the author, to avoid mentioning the same places of encampment a second time,” for any such plan is a mere conjecture; but it may be simply and perfectly explained from the fact, that on this return route-which the whole of the people, with their wives, children, and flocks, could accomplish without any very great exertion in ten or fourteen days, as the distance from Aila to Kadesh through the desert of Paran is only about a forty hours’ journey upon camels, and Robinson travelled from Akabah to the Wady Retemath, near Kadesh, in four days and a half-no formal camp was pitched at all, probably because the time of penal wandering came to an end at Eziongeber, and the time had arrived when the congregation was to assemble again at Kadesh, and set out thence upon its journey to Canaan. - Hence the eleven names given in Num 33:19-30, between <hi type="italic">Rithmah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Moseroth</hi>, can only refer to those stations at which the congregation pitched their camp for a longer or shorter period during the thirty-seven years of punishment, on their slow return from Kadesh to the Red Sea, and previous to their entering the Arabah and encamping at Moseroth. <div eID="gen2068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2069" type="x-p"/> This number of stations, which is very small for thirty-seven years (only seventeen from Rithmah or Kadesh to Eziongeber), is a sufficient proof that the congregation of Israel was not constantly wandering about during the whole of that time, but may have remained in many of the places of encampment, probably those which furnished an abundant supply of water and pasturage, not only for weeks and months, but even for years, the people scattering themselves in all directions round about the place where the tabernacle was set up, and making use of such means of support as the desert afforded, and assembling together again when this was all gone, for the purpose of travelling farther and seeking somewhere else a suitable spot for a fresh encampment. Moreover, the words of <reference osisRef="Deut.1.46">Deu 1:46</reference>, “ye abode in Kadesh many days,” when compared with Num 2:1, “then we turned, and took our journey into the wilderness of the way to the Red Sea,” show most distinctly, that after the sentence passed upon the people in Kadesh (Num 14), they did not begin to travel back at once, but remained for a considerable time in Kadesh before going southwards into the desert. <div eID="gen2069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2070" type="x-p"/> With regard to the direction which they took, all that can be said, so long as none of the places of encampment mentioned in Num 33:19-29 are discovered, is that they made their way by a very circuitous route, and with many a wide detour, to Eziongeber, on the Red Sea.<note placement="foot">We agree so far, therefore, with the vie adopted by <hi type="italic">Fries</hi>, and followed by <hi type="italic">Kurtz</hi> (History of Old Covenant, iii. 306-7) and <hi type="italic">Schultz</hi> (Deut. pp. 153-4), that we regard the stations given in vv. 19-35, between <hi type="italic">Rithmah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Eziongeber</hi>, as referring to the journeys of Israel, after its condemnation in Kadesh, during the thirty-seven years of its wandering about in the desert. But we do not regard the view which these writers have formed of the marches themselves as being well founded, or in accordance with the text, - namely, that the people of Israel did not really come a second time in full procession from the south to Kadesh, but that they had never left Kadesh entirely, inasmuch as then the nation was rejected in Kadesh, the people divided themselves into larger and smaller groups, and that portion which was estranged from Moses, or rather from the Lord, remained in Kadesh even after the rest were scattered about; so that, in a certain sense, Kadesh formed the standing encampment and meeting-place of the congregation even during the thirty-seven years. According to this view, the removals and encampments mentioned in vv. 9-36 do not describe the marches of the whole nation, but are to be understood as the circuit made by the headquarters during the thirty-seven years, with Moses at the head and the sanctuary in the midst (<hi type="italic">Kurtz</hi>), or else as showing “that Moses and Aaron, with the sanctuary and the tribe of Levi, altered their resting-place, say from year to year, thus securing to every part of the nation in turn the nearness of the sanctuary, in accordance with the signals appointed by God (Num 10:11-12), and thus passed over the space between Kadesh and Eziongeber within the first eighteen years, and then, by a similar change of place, gradually drew near to Kadesh during the remaining eighteen or nineteen years, and at length in the last year summoned the whole nation (all the congregation) to assemble together at this meeting-place.” Now we cannot admit that in this view “we find all the different and scattered statements of the Pentateuch explained and rendered intelligible.” In the first place, it does not do justice even to the list of stations; for if the constantly repeated expression, “and they (the children of Israel, Num 33:1) removed...and encamped,” denotes the removal and encamping of the whole congregation in vv. 3-18 and Num 33:37-49, it is certainly at variance with the text to explain the same words in vv. 19-36 as signifying the removal and encamping of the headquarters only, or of Moses, with Aaron and the Levites, and the tabernacle. Again, in all the laws that were given and the events that are described as occurring between the first halt of the congregation in Kadesh (Num 13 and 14) and their return thither at the commencement of the fortieth year (Num 20), the presence of the whole congregation is taken for granted. The sacrificial laws in Num 15, which Moses was to address to the children of Israel (Num 15:1), were given to “the whole congregation” (cf. Num 33:24, Num 33:25, Num 33:26). The man who gathered wood on the Sabbath was taken out of the camp and stoned by “all the congregation” (Num 15:36). “All the congregation” took part in the rebellion of the company of Korah (Num 16:19; Num 17:6, Num 18:8.). It is true this occurrence is supposed by <hi type="italic">Kurtz</hi> to have taken place “during the halt in Kadesh,” but the reasons given are by no means conclusive (p. 105). Besides, if we assign everything that is related in Num 15-19 to the time when the whole congregation abode in Kadesh, this deprives the hypothesis of its chief support in <reference osisRef="Deut.1.46">Deu 1:46</reference>, “and ye abode in Kadesh a long time, according to the days that he abode.” For in that case the long abode in Kadesh would include the period of the laws and incidents recorded in Num 15-19, and yet, after all, “the whole congregation” went away. In no case, in fact, can the words be understood as signifying that a portion of the nation remained there during the thirty-seven years. Nor can this be inferred in any way from the fact that their departure is not expressly mentioned; for, at all events, the statement in Num 20:1, “and the children of Israel, the whole congregation, came into the desert of Zin,” presupposes that they had gone away. And the “inconceivable idea, that in the last year of their wanderings, when it was their express intention to cross the Jordan and enter Canaan from the east, they should have gone up from Eziongeber to the southern boundary of Canaan, which they had left thirty-seven years before, merely to come back again to the neighbourhood of Eziongeber, after failing in their negotiations with the king of Edom, which they might have carried on from some place much farther south, and to take the road from that point to the country on the east of the Jordan after all” (<hi type="italic">Fries</hi>), loses all the surprising character which it apparently has, if we only give up the assumption upon which it is founded, but which has no support whatever in the biblical history, viz., that during the thirty-seven years of their wandering in the desert, Moses was acquainted with the fact that the Israelites were to enter Canaan from the east, or at any rate that he had formed this plan for some time. If, on the contrary, when the Lord rejected the murmuring nation (Num 14:26), He decided nothing with reference to the way by which the generation that would grow up in the desert was to enter Canaan, - and it was not till after the return to Kadesh that Moses was informed by God that they were to advance into Canaan from the east and not from the south, - it was perfectly natural that when the time of punishment had expired, the Israelites should assemble in Kadesh again, and start from that point upon their journey onward.</note>

XXXVI. 13.</title> <div sID="gen2072" type="x-p"/> These instructions, with which the eyes of the Israelites were directed to the end of all their wandering, viz., the possession of the promised land, are arranged in two sections by longer introductory formulas (Num 33:50 and Num 35:1). The former contains the divine commands (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) with regard to the extermination of the Canaanites and their idolatry, and the division of the land among the tribes of Israel (Num 33:50-56); (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) concerning the boundaries of Canaan (Num 34:1-15); (<hi type="italic">c</hi>) concerning the men who were to divide the land (Num 34:16-29). The second contains commands (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) respecting the towns to be given up to the Levites (Num 35:1-8); (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) as to the setting apart of cities of refuge for unintentional manslayers, and the course to be adopted in relation to such manslayers (Num 35:9-34); and (<hi type="italic">c</hi>) a law concerning the marrying of heiresses within their own tribes (Num 36:1-13). - The careful dovetailing of all these legal regulations by separate introductory formulas, is a distinct proof that the section Num 33:50-56 is not to be regarded, as <hi type="italic">Baumgarten</hi>, <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>, and others suppose, in accordance with the traditional division of the chapters, as an appendix or admonitory conclusion to the list of stations, but as the general legal foundation for the more minute instructions in Num 34-36.
